Live evidence for perles-net-k3j.2 (S4), captured 2026-08-23 against
codex-cli 0.149.0.

Question: does notify's `cwd` resolve the workspace, and does `thread-id`
match the `session_start` session id?

=== cwd resolution ===

`codex exec` was invoked with cwd =
/tmp/claude-1000/.../scratchpad/k3j2/run1 (a scratch workspace directory).
The captured notify payload's `cwd` field is exactly that directory:

  payload.notify.agent-turn-complete.json: "cwd":
  "/tmp/claude-1000/-home-pascal-perles-net/5c8d83e3-54d9-4e9d-a620-a533a0cd4f3d/scratchpad/k3j2/run1"

Confirmed: `cwd` in the notify payload is the process's actual working
directory at invocation time, i.e. it resolves the workspace the same way
Claude's SessionStart/hook payloads do. Not exercised: `-C`/`--cd` or
`--add-dir` overrides, or a symlinked/relative workspace path.

=== thread-id vs session_start session id ===

A direct live SessionStart-hook correlation could not be captured this
spike: adding a second hooks.json SessionStart hook-group (co-existing with
the pre-existing herdr entry, following S1's documented pattern of multiple
hook groups per event) never acquired the silent one-run trust delay that
perles-net-k3j.1's spike observed for a brand-new event registration --
across 4 codex exec invocations (2 different cwd, including one from an
already-`trust_level = "trusted"` project) spanning warm-up + real runs, no
new `[hooks.state]` entry was ever written to config.toml for the added
hook, and the hook script never fired (its capture file was never created).
This is recorded as NOT DETERMINED this spike (see "what could not be
determined" below); hooks.json was restored byte-identical regardless (see
findings comment).

Correlation was instead established through the on-disk rollout transcript,
which is Codex's own durable record of session identity and is written
independent of any hook:

  Notify payload (run1, turn 1): "thread-id":
  "01a02e51-c257-75c3-b242-b56199a18839"

  Rollout file located by that exact id:
  ~/.codex/sessions/2026/08/23/rollout-2026-08-23T13-11-45-01a02e51-c257-75c3-b242-b56199a18839.jsonl

  First record in that file:
  {"type":"session_meta","payload":{"session_id":"01a02e51-c257-75c3-b242-b56199a18839","id":"01a02e51-c257-75c3-b242-b56199a18839", ...}}

  Also matches the `codex exec --json` stream's own ground truth:
  {"type":"thread.started","thread_id":"01a02e51-c257-75c3-b242-b56199a18839"}

perles-net-k3j.1's SessionStart fixture (payload.session-start.json) shows
the hook's session-identity field is literally named `session_id`
(`"session_id": "01a02e46-9486-7ef3-9af5-282ebecc6329"`), the same field
name the rollout's session_meta payload uses. Since the rollout filename,
session_meta.payload.session_id, the `codex exec --json` stream's
thread_id, and the notify payload's thread-id are all the identical value
for the same session in every run captured this spike (5 separate live
sessions, 2 of them multi-turn via resume), thread-id and session_id are the
same identifier under two different field names across two different
mechanisms (notify vs hooks.json), not independently-assigned values that
merely happen to correlate. This satisfies S4's question via an equally
strong evidentiary path (Codex's own durable session record) even though
the live SessionStart-hook capture itself did not fire.

=== Session-id / thread-id format ===

All 6 distinct thread-ids observed this spike (S2 exercises) and in S1's
fixtures are 36-character canonical UUID strings whose version nibble
(first hex digit of the 3rd group) is consistently `7`:

  01a02e51-c257-75c3-... 01a02e51-c2d5-7931-... 01a02e53-e701-7cd3-...
  01a02e55-0354-7942-... 01a02e57-0c41-7f20-... 01a02e57-97d7-72a2-...
  01a02e58-4c91-72a0-... (S2, this spike)
  01a02e46-9486-7ef3-... (S1 fixture, perles-net-k3j.1)

-> UUIDv7 (time-ordered: the leading 48 bits are a millisecond Unix
timestamp, which is why successive ids captured seconds apart sort
lexically increasing, e.g. 01a02e51 < 01a02e53 < 01a02e55 < 01a02e57 <
01a02e58 across this session). UUIDv7 carries 74 bits of randomness
(62 random bits + monotonic-within-millisecond counter bits depending on
implementation), so the plan's composite-key rationale ("effectively-unique
ids") holds for Codex thread/session ids: collision probability across any
realistic number of sessions on one machine is negligible, same class of
guarantee as Claude's session ids. Not verified: the exact bit layout
(random vs counter) of Codex's specific UUIDv7 generator, and turn-ids use
the same UUIDv7 shape but were not separately analyzed for uniqueness
properties since S2/S4 only asked about session/thread ids.
